Correction: the earlier version said the model was not explicitly labelled |

| **Reviewer recommendations** | Reviewers assess fit, content, structure, style and impact and give formative feedback plus a publication recommendation; opinion pieces and reviews are usually not peer-reviewed unless they include original research |

> Source: https://www.imprint.co.uk/peer-review-policy/ (page dated 2026-09-29, retrieved 2026-11-23) and https://www.imprint.co.uk/jcs-authors-guide/. Editor-authored papers are assigned to another editor for all tasks (same policy page).

### AI Policy

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Has journal-specific AI policy?** | Publisher-wide policy for Imprint Academic books and journals, which the JCS authors' guide links and enforces: every submission must come with a declaration that the policy was complied with |
| **Explicit permission gate?** | conditional: AI is allowed only for readability and language, with disclosure |
| **Leniency (1-5)** | 2 |
| **Summary** | Policy PDF (read 2026-11-23): generative AI may be used only to improve readability and language, not to create content, produce insights, draw scientific or philosophical conclusions or generate content from an author's initial ideas; use must be disclosed in the manuscript and a statement appears in the published work. Editors may use AI-detector software at the preview stage and may investigate submissions. AI cannot be listed or cited as an author. Reviewers must not generate review reports with AI and may only polish them; editors must not use AI to summarise papers or reviews. The policy covers the writing process, not AI use for data analysis. The JCS guide asks for a 150-word summary and for confirmation of compliance placed within the paper |

## Format

Source for this section: https://www.imprint.co.uk/jcs-authors-guide/ (retrieved 2026-11-23) and https://www.imprint.co.uk/journal-submissions/ (same date).

| Aspect | Detail |
|--------|--------|
| **Article types accepted** | Stand-alone academic papers; the journal does not publish very short research notes or letters to the editor; books for review go to a Book Reviews Editor; themed sections and symposia with commentaries and replies appear in print (see Publication Frequency) |
| **Word limit** | 9,000 words including abstract, footnotes and references; the guide says the vast majority of papers are 5,000-9,000 words; very brief contributions will not usually be considered |
| **Word limit negotiability** | Stated as the upper limit; no exception route is described on the page |
| **Abstract limit** | A 150-word summary at the start of the paper |
| **Reference limit** | No numeric limit; Harvard system with DOIs where available |
| **Supplementary material** | Not mentioned. Figures and tables go in the main submission file |
| **Figure/Table limits** | No numeric limit stated; on acceptance authors supply alt text, 25-30 words (maximum 100) |

### Orientation

> Keyword counts below are from Crossref records for ISSN 1355-8250 and 2051-2201, journal articles from 2021-01 to 2026-11-23: 372 articles, of which 310 (83%) carry a deposited abstract, retrieved 2026-11-23. Crossref holds no records for this ISSN before 2021, so the window is effectively the whole of 2021-2026. Keywords were matched locally in title plus abstract, shares are of the 310 with abstracts, and all counts are lower bounds. OpenAlex `works` queries were not available (daily budget exhausted).

| Dimension | Assessment |
|-----------|------------|
| **Empirical vs. Theoretical** | Theoretical argument is the largest strand: "argu*" in 146 of 310 abstracts (47.1%), "philosoph*" 63 (20.3%). Empirical and scientific strands are visible: "neuro*/fMRI/EEG/brain" 64 (20.6%), "empirical" 21 (6.8%), "experiment*" 12 (3.9%), "participants" 11 (3.5%) |
| **Quantitative vs. Qualitative** | "qualitative" 14 (4.5%), "interview" 6 (1.9%), "survey/questionnaire" 5 (1.6%), "case study" 4 (1.3%); first-person or micro-phenomenological terms 41 (13.2%) |
| **Cross-disciplinary openness** | The publisher describes a multidisciplinary peer-reviewed journal examining the mind-brain relation, machine consciousness, subjectivity and the self "in plain English" (https://www.imprint.co.uk/product/jcs/). Counts: physics ("quantum") 22 (7.1%), psychology 35 (11.3%), cognitive science 8 (2.6%), spiritual/mystical/religious terms 21 (6.8%), Eastern-tradition terms 17 (5.5%), animal/non-human 28 (9.0%), AI/language-model terms 21 (6.8%) |

**Current positioning (what the journal accepts now):** the 2026 issues carry a themed section on AI consciousness ("Introduction: Consciousness in Current AI", DOI 10.53765/20512201.33.7.009, with papers on global workspace theory and language agents, on artificial affective consciousness and on temporal continuity in LLMs), a 2026 editorial on "Superpsychism" (10.53765/20512201.33.1.009), a 2026 section on mind, music and mental health (10.53765/20512201.33.3.010), and papers on near-death and out-of-body experience and on quantum approaches (10.53765/20512201.33.9.111, 10.53765/20512201.33.9.060, 10.53765/20512201.33.9.007). The earlier note on the Bohm special issue is retained and dated: a call for papers was posted 2024-02-23 (see Publication Frequency).

**Methods noted as welcome (qualitative — not a scored 0-5 table, see Methodological Preferences below):** philosophical argument about consciousness; theory papers that join philosophy with neuroscience, physics or psychology; first-person and phenomenological methods; qualitative studies of anomalous or contemplative experience; symposium and author-meets-critics formats with commentaries and replies.

## Soft Metadata

### Epistemological & Political Leanings

- Scope statement: the publisher describes the journal as multidisciplinary and peer-reviewed, examining questions such as how the mind relates to the brain and whether computers can be conscious (https://www.imprint.co.uk/product/jcs/, retrieved 2026-11-23); no political or epistemological stance is stated on the pages read.
- Positions named in titles/abstracts of 310 articles with abstracts, 2021-2026 (Crossref, retrieved 2026-11-23): panpsychism 38 (12.3%), physicalism or materialism 29 (9.4%), dualism 20 (6.5%), idealism 6 (1.9%), illusionism 6 (1.9%), integrated information theory 10 (3.2%), global workspace or higher-order theories 9 (2.9%), quantum approaches 22 (7.1%), phenomenological terms 37 (11.9%).
- Named figures: Bohm 9 (2.9%), Chalmers/Dennett/Nagel 10 (3.2%), Husserl/Heidegger/Merleau-Ponty 7 (2.3%), Kant 1.
- Special-issue statement by a guest editor, 2024-02-23: Bohm's implicate order was not well regarded in physics, while later developments make his work look more prescient than marginal (https://ctr4process.org/call-for-papers-the-legacy-of-david-bohm-journal-of-consciousness-studies/); this is the guest editor's framing of one issue, not a journal-wide stance.
- Editorial Advisory Board includes D. Chalmers, C. Koch, K. Friston, R. Penrose, S. Hameroff, P. Goff and E. Schwitzgebel among 27 names (https://www.imprint.co.uk/product/jcs/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Reading of the counts: the published pattern is pluralist, with mainstream consciousness science, analytic metaphysics (physicalist, dualist, panpsychist), phenomenology and quantum or contemplative approaches all present; no single position exceeds about 12% of abstracts. This describes what is published, not editors' politics.

### Framing Requirements

- Mandatory framing: papers must be accessible to an educated multidisciplinary readership; authors should not assume specialist knowledge, should give background, avoid or explain technical terms, and place technical detail in footnotes or appendices, and likewise for mathematics unless essential (https://www.imprint.co.uk/jcs-authors-guide/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Article form: stand-alone academic papers of up to 9,000 words including abstract, footnotes and references, mostly 5,000-9,000; no short research notes or letters; a 150-word summary at the start (same URL).
- One paper at a time: authors may have only one paper under consideration, and multiple submissions are not permitted (https://www.imprint.co.uk/journal-submissions/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Themed sections: 16 of 372 Crossref titles are introductions, editorials or symposia and 27 are commentaries or replies (own count, retrieved 2026-11-23), so part of the output is organised around invited themes.
- Consequence of ignoring the framing: the policy says submissions are first desk-assessed for suitability for peer review (https://www.imprint.co.uk/peer-review-policy/); no rejection statistics are given.

### Methodological Preferences

Scoring rule (this pass's own convention, not the journal's): hits divided by the 310 articles with abstracts, 2021-2026; 0 gives 0, under 1% gives 1, 1-5% gives 2, over 5% gives 3. Scores of 4-5 need a cited editorial statement and none was found. Source: Crossref titles/abstracts for ISSN 1355-8250, retrieved 2026-11-23; counts are lower bounds.

| Method | Receptiveness (0-5) | Evidence |
|--------|---------------------|----------|
| Philosophical argument / conceptual analysis | 3 | "argu*" 146 articles (47.1%), "philosoph*" 63 (20.3%); capped at 3 by rule |
| Neuroscience / brain-based work | 3 | "neuro*, fMRI, EEG, brain" 64 articles (20.6%) |
| Computational / modelling | 3 | "computational" or "model" 45 articles (14.5%); the term "model" also appears in purely theoretical papers, so this overstates computational work |
| First-person / phenomenological methods | 3 | "micro-phenomenology, first-person, introspection" 41 articles (13.2%); "phenomenolog*" 37 (11.9%) |
| Physics / quantum approaches | 3 | "quantum" 22 articles (7.1%) |
| Empirical studies (general) | 3 | "empirical" 21 articles (6.8%) |
| Behavioural experiments | 2 | "experiment*" 12 articles (3.9%) |
| Qualitative methods | 2 | "qualitative" 14 articles (4.5%), e.g. a phenomenological qualitative study of out-of-body experiences (DOI 10.53765/20512201.33.9.060) |
| Interviews | 2 | 6 articles (1.9%) |
| Survey / questionnaire | 2 | 5 articles (1.6%) |
| Mathematical / formal | 2 | "mathemat*, formal" 15 articles (4.8%) |
| Case study | 2 | 4 articles (1.3%); some are philosophical or single-agent cases, e.g. DOI 10.53765/20512201.33.7.014 |

### Voice & Style

- Stated style: plain, accessible writing for non-specialists; technical terms avoided or explained; Harvard references with DOIs; quotations over six lines indented (https://www.imprint.co.uk/jcs-authors-guide/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- The publisher describes the journal as examining its questions "in plain English" (https://www.imprint.co.uk/product/jcs/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Authorship pattern: 276 of 370 articles with author data (75%) have a single author (Crossref, own count, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- First-person use in titles/abstracts (310 articles with abstracts, Crossref, retrieved 2026-11-23): "I" in 146 (47.1%), "we" in 128 (41.3%), "my" or "our" in 88 (28.4%); "this paper/article/essay" in 137 (44.2%). Examples: "We challenge this assumption" (DOI 10.53765/20512201.33.7.061), "I contend that" (10.53765/20512201.33.9.161).
- Recent openings sampled (DOIs): 10.53765/20512201.33.7.035 opens with a development in the field ("Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have reignited questions..."); 10.53765/20512201.33.9.031 opens with a clinical fact about psychedelic therapy; 10.53765/20512201.33.9.060 opens by defining the phenomenon ("Out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are vivid and extraordinary events..."); 10.53765/20512201.33.9.111 opens with a claim about physicalism; 10.53765/20512201.33.7.097 opens "We explore and argue for the view".

### Reviewer Pool Characteristics

- Review model: double-blind, at least two subject experts, who may include editorial advisory board members (https://www.imprint.co.uk/peer-review-policy/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Board counts (https://www.imprint.co.uk/product/jcs/, retrieved 2026-11-23): Editor-in-Chief, Managing Editor (publisher staff), Book Reviews Editor, Associate Editor, 5 Founding Editors (one deceased), and 27 Editorial Advisory Board members; of the 27, 15 list a US institution, 7 UK, 2 Canada, 1 France, 1 Finland/Sweden, 1 no country (own count).
- Disciplines are not labelled on the page; the names include philosophers, neuroscientists and physicists (e.g. Chalmers, Friston, Penrose, Rovelli), which is a reading of the names, not a stated classification.
- OpenAlex-derived topic mix of the journal's output (spine, 2026-07-13): Philosophy and Theoretical Science 139, Embodied and Extended Cognition 115, Paranormal Experiences and Beliefs 100, Quantum Mechanics and Applications 58 topic assignments.
- Reviewer turnaround asked by the publisher: 5-6 weeks (peer-review policy URL above).
- APA Journal Survey (self-reported, n=24): average 2 reviewers, 87.5% of submissions received comments; no submitter comment text was given in the 24 entries (https://apasurvey.philx.org/journals/503, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Reviewer behaviour itself (tone, expectations) is not observable from public pages.

### Practical Concerns

- Submission route: by email to the Managing Editor as a Word, RTF or PDF attachment, with figures and tables inside the file; fully blinded; a short author CV/bio paragraph is requested (https://www.imprint.co.uk/jcs-authors-guide/, retrieved 2026-11-23). The page states that by submitting, authors consent to the JCS email newsletter, with an opt-out on request (https://www.imprint.co.uk/journal-submissions/).
- Ethics: for human-participant studies a statement naming the approving ethics committee and informed-consent confirmation is required; animal studies need a statement of ethical approval in the Methods; COPE guidance is followed (https://www.imprint.co.uk/publishing-ethics/, retrieved 2026-11-23).
- Data: a data availability statement is required, with repository link and data citation where data are shared; sharing is not expected where it would breach ethical or legal requirements (same page).
- Declarations and checks: competing-interest declaration ("none" if none); authorship criteria listed on the page; originality check with Crossref Similarity Check (same page).
- Preprints: allowed with disclosure on the title page; accepted-manuscript posting delayed 24 months on the subscription route (https://www.imprint.co.uk/publishing-ethics/ and https://www.imprint.co.uk/open-access/).
- OA and charges: no charge on the subscription route; gold OA GBP 1,500 excluding VAT, CC-BY (https://www.imprint.co.uk/open-access/).
- AI: policy declaration required with every submission (URL in the AI Policy table).
- Independent-scholar rules: none stated on the pages read. One of the 24 entries in the APA Journal Survey lists an independent scholar with a conditional-acceptance verdict (https://apasurvey.philx.org/journals/503), a single anecdote.

## Strategic Notes

> Every statement below follows from a fact recorded above and names it. Judgements about the journal's culture are not made because the evidence for them is absent.

### Hard Blockers

- A non-anonymised manuscript: anonymised submissions are mandatory and review is double-blind (Peer Review, Format).
- A paper over 9,000 words including abstract, footnotes and references, or a very short note or letter (Format table).
- Several JCS submissions at once: only one paper under consideration per author (Framing Requirements).
- AI use beyond readability and language, or a missing compliance declaration (AI Policy table).
- Work that cannot be read by a non-specialist: the guide requires an accessible, multidisciplinary text (Framing Requirements).

### Soft Tax

- Writing for non-specialists: technical detail has to move into footnotes or appendices, which still count toward 9,000 words (Framing Requirements, Format).
- Subscription-route embargo: the accepted manuscript cannot be posted for 24 months after publication unless the institution has a rights-retention policy; gold OA costs GBP 1,500 plus VAT (Preprint Policy, Open Access).
- Timeline: only a target (5-6 weeks to referee recommendation) and an n=24 self-reported 3.2-month average response are available, so no reliable estimate exists (Review Cycle Time).

### Best Suited For

- Single-author theoretical or interdisciplinary papers on consciousness: 75% of articles are single-authored and "argu*" appears in 47.1% of abstracts (Orientation, Voice & Style).
- Work that joins philosophy with neuroscience, physics, psychology or contemplative traditions: neuro-terms 20.6%, quantum 7.1%, Eastern-tradition terms 5.5% (Orientation, Sensitive Topics).
- Papers on AI and machine consciousness: 21 articles (6.8%) and a 2026 themed section (Orientation).
- Papers on anomalous or contemplative experience and first-person methods: first-person terms 13.2%, spiritual terms 6.8%, near-death or paranormal terms 3.2% (Methodological Preferences, Sensitive Topics).

### Not Recommended For

- Papers centred on race, gender or political analysis of consciousness research: 3 articles (1.0%) in 310 (Sensitive Topics); this is rarity, not a stated exclusion.
- Large survey or experimental studies: "survey" 1.6% and "experiment*" 3.9% of abstracts (Methodological Preferences); a technical report with heavy methods does not fit the plain-English requirement (Framing Requirements).
- Authors who need open-access preprint availability of the accepted manuscript soon after acceptance and do not pay: the subscription route imposes a 24-month delay (Preprint Policy).

### Rejection Fallback Chain

| Rank | Journal | Why this fallback works |
|------|---------|------------------------|
| 1 | [Consciousness and Cognition](../cognitive-science/consciousness-and-cognition.md) | In the corpus; same subject area, see that entry for its own data |
| 2 | [Neuroscience of Consciousness](../cognitive-science/neuroscience-of-consciousness.md) | In the corpus; for papers with a neuroscience component (20.6% of JCS abstracts match neuro-terms), see that entry |
| 3 | [Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences](../psychology/phenomenology-and-the-cognitive-sciences.md) | In the corpus; for phenomenological papers (11.9% of JCS abstracts), see that entry |
| 4 | [Mind & Language](./mind-and-language.md) | In the corpus; for philosophy-of-mind arguments, see that entry |
